sentences.text: Nemegtosaurus was a sauropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous Period.
Scientists estimated this giant animal to measure between 12 and 13 meters long and weigh 20 tonnes.
The genus was named after the Nemegt Basin in the Gobi Desert, where only a single skull was found.
The skull of Nemegtosaurus was long and low, resembling diplodocoids, and possessed pencil-shaped teeth.
An adult Nemegtosaurus, with a possible length of 12 meters, may have been able to defend itself against Tarbosaurus, while juveniles would have been vulnerable.
A second species, N. pachi, was described by Dong in 1977 based on teeth from the Subashi Formation, but it is considered a nomen dubium.
Like other titanosaurs, Nemegtosaurus had slender, pencil-like teeth ground to a sharp, chisel-like tip.
It is unclear whether Nemegtosaurus browsed high in trees or grazed on low plants, as related titanosaurs exhibit both feeding strategies.
Recent studies have classified Nemegtosaurus as a titanosaur closely related to Saltasaurus, Alamosaurus, and Rapetosaurus.
Nemegtosaurus is classified within the family Saltasauridae.
Nemegtosaurus belongs to the subfamily Nemegtosaurinae.
Nemegtosaurus acquired its current status as a titanosaur in the subfamily Nemegtosaurinae within Saltasauridae after 2004.
Nemegtosaurus lived in the Maastrichtian (66-72 million years ago) Nemegt Formation, making it one of the last sauropods on Earth.
Nemegtosaurus lived on a lush river delta in the Gobi Desert alongside animals such as Gallimimus, Mononykus, Adasaurus, Therizinosaurus, and Tarbosaurus.
Nemegtosaurus lived at the end of the Cretaceous Period, approximately 83 to 65 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
The time range for Nemegtosaurus is estimated from the Coniacian to the Maastrichtian (89.8 to 66 million years ago).
In 2019, Averianov and Lopatin determined that Nemegtosaurus and Opisthocoelicaudia were not synonymous because shared characters were difficult to determine or based on misidentified specimens.
It has been proposed that the skull actually belongs to Opisthocoelicaudia, although the postcranial skeleton of that genus clearly belongs to a different family.
The rediscovery of the Nemegtosaurus type locality and discovery of comparable postcranial remains have reopened the debate that Opisthocoelicaudia might be a junior synonym of Nemegtosaurus.
